# New house renderings introduced in odyssey-023 (Odyssey 5.97–191)

For folding into `conventions.md`'s house-renderings table at publication.

| Greek | `l` | `i` | avoided on purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| πολύτλας (standing epithet of Odysseus, 5.171) | "much-enduring" | "much-enduring" | "long-suffering" (drops πολυ- "much" and adds a meek, patient tone the word does not have), "much-suffering" ("suffering" belongs to the πάσχω family, as in ἄλγεα πάσχων; τλάω is "endure, bear up under"), "steadfast" (already the `i` of ταλασίφρων, and a claim about moral character where the Greek says literally what he has borne), "enduring-minded" (reserved for ταλασίφρων; "-minded" belongs to the -φρων epithets), "patient". Same root as ταλασίφρων and τλαίης (5.178), and the note points this out |
| πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς (whole name-formula, line-end, 5.171) | "much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus" | "much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus" | dropping either epithet; "divine" for δῖος (reserved for θεῖος); reordering the epithets round the name ("heavenly Odysseus, the much-enduring") |
| ὣς φάτο, ῥίγησεν δὲ [Name] (reaction-formula after a speech, 5.116 of Calypso, 5.171 of Odysseus) | "So he/she spoke, and shuddered, [Name]," | "So he/she spoke, and [Name] shuddered," | "was dismayed", "was troubled", "was alarmed" (each loses the bodily chill of ῥιγέω, from ῥῖγος "cold, frost"), "trembled" (keep for τρέω / τρομέω), "shivered" (sounds like cold weather). Built on the shipped pattern of ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ [Name] ("So he spoke, and smiled, [Name],", 4.609) |
| ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη/ἱστάμενος + verb of speaking (5.159 with προσεφώνεε; cf. the shipped ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα, 4.25) | "And standing close by, …" | "came and stood close beside him/her, and …" | "approaching" (drops ἵστημι), "addressed" for προσεφώνεε (reserved for προσέειπε / προσέφη; προσφωνέω is "spoke to") |
| [ἀλλὰ μάλ’ / ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ] οὔ πως ἔστι Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο / οὔτε παρεξελθεῖν ἄλλον θεὸν οὔθ’ ἁλιῶσαι (two-line formula, 5.103–104 = 5.137–138 except for the opening words) | "[But there is no way at all / But since there is no way] that the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus / any other god should either slip past or bring to nothing" | "… for any other god to slip past the mind of aegis-bearing Zeus or bring it to nothing" | "thwart", "circumvent", "cross" (lose the literal παρ-εξ-ελθεῖν "go out past"), "make void" / "frustrate" alone (lose ἅλιος "fruitless, vain", kept as "bring to nothing"), "will" or "purpose" for νόος (the pilot's "mind") |
| ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἀπέφθιθεν ἐσθλοὶ ἑταῖροι, / τὸν δ’ ἄρα δεῦρ’ ἄνεμός τε φέρων καὶ κῦμα πέλασσε. (two whole lines, 5.110–111 = 5.133–134) | "There all the others perished, his good companions, / but him, then, the wind, bearing him, and the wave brought near to here." | "There all his other good companions perished, but the wind and the wave carried him and brought him here." | "noble companions" (ἐσθλός is kept "good", as in ἐσθλὸς Ὀδυσσεύς "good Odysseus", 3.98, 4.328), "washed him ashore" (drops πελάζω "bring near") |
| μή τί μοι/τοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο (whole line, 5.179 and 5.187 with μοι / τοι) | "that you/I will not plan some other evil woe against me/you myself/yourself" | "that you/I will not plan some other evil woe against me/you" | "harm" / "mischief" alone (πῆμα is kept "woe", as shipped for πήματα at 3.100); "plot" (keep for λοχάω / δόλος words); the future sense of βουλευσέμεν is kept |
| ἴστω νῦν τόδε γαῖα καὶ οὐρανὸς εὐρὺς ὕπερθε / καὶ τὸ κατειβόμενον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ, ὅς τε μέγιστος / ὅρκος δεινότατός τε πέλει μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι (the gods' oath by the Styx, 5.184–186) | "Let now the earth know this, and the wide sky above, / and the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the greatest / oath and the most dread for the blessed gods," | "Now let the earth know this, and the wide sky above, and the down-flowing water of the Styx, which is the greatest and most dread oath for the blessed gods," | "be my witness" (the verb is οἶδα, "know"), "the dread river Styx" (the Greek names its water, ὕδωρ), "falling water" / "cascading" for κατειβόμενον (kept "down-flowing", the same verb as κατείβετο "was ebbing away" at 5.152) |
| χρυσόθρονος (of Artemis, 5.123) | "golden-throned" | "golden-throned" (+ note: an old alternative derives the second part from θρόνα "embroidered flowers") | "of the golden flowers" or "golden-robed" as if certain; "gold-enthroned" |
| Ἄρτεμις ἁγνή (5.123) | "Artemis the pure" | "Artemis the pure" | "holy" (reserved for ἠγάθεος, "holy Pylos"), "sacred" (ἱερός), "chaste" (narrows ἁγνός to a sexual sense) |
| ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ (5.128, 5.131) | "with the bright thunderbolt" | "with the bright thunderbolt" | "flashing" (the table already turns it down for αἴθων and γλαυκῶπις), "shining" (keep for φαεινός), "white" (literal to the root ἀργ- but misleading in English), "vivid"; kept distinct from the shipped κύνες ἀργοί "swift dogs", a different adjective on the same root |
| θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες (5.122; shipped at 4.805) | "the gods who live at ease" | "the gods who live at ease" | "the easy-living gods", "the blessed gods" (that is μάκαρες) |
| [οἷς] ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχόμενος/ἐποιχομένη κατέπεφνε(ν) (5.124, fem., of Artemis; shipped masc. at 3.280, of Apollo) | "with his/her gentle shafts assailing, slew" | "came upon … with his/her gentle arrows and killed …" | "kindly arrows", "painless darts" (the note, not the translation, says the death is sudden and painless) |
| μίγη / μιγῆναι φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ (5.126) | "was mingled in love and in bed" | "lay in love with …" | "made love", "slept with" (flatten μίγνυμι "mix, mingle"), "was joined" |
| κάμμορε (vocative address, 5.160) | "Ill-fated one" | "Ill-fated man" | "wretch", "poor fool", "unlucky one", "unhappy man" (κάμμορος = κατάμορος, built on μόρος "portion": "ill-fated" keeps the root) |
| νῆες ἐῖσαι ὠκύποροι (5.175–176) | "well-balanced ships, swift-faring" | "well-balanced, swift-faring ships" | "sea-going", "fast-sailing", "quick-passaged"; ὠκύς keeps the table's "swift", πόρος "passage, faring"; ἐῖσαι keeps the table's "well-balanced" |
| πρόφρων (of a willing helper, 5.143; shipped at 2.230 as "ready-minded"), with the epic feminine πρόφρασσα (5.161) | "ready-minded" | "with a ready mind" | "gladly", "eagerly", "kindly" (lose φρήν), "wholeheartedly" |

## Extension of an existing fixed rendering

- **χειρί τέ μιν κατέρεξεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν** (4.610, fixed; 5.181 exact repeat of the Greek line) — shipped with a male subject as "and stroked him with his hand, …". At 5.181 the subject is Calypso, so the English reads "and stroked him with her hand, …" in both layers. χειρί has no possessive in the Greek, so only the English pronoun follows the speaker's sex, exactly as the table's ὣς φάτο row already does for "So he/she spoke". The unit's Greek differs from the published unit (different first line), so the validator's whole-unit rule is not touched.
- **καί μιν φωνήσας(’) ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα** — both shipped wordings are reused verbatim: the feminine at 5.117 ("and, lifting her voice, to him winged words she spoke:" / "and, raising her voice, spoke winged words to him:") and the masculine at 5.172 ("and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:" / "and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:"). The two shipped `i` wordings differ slightly in commas and verb ("raising" / "lifting"). I left them as shipped, and flag the difference here.

## Flags for the reviewer (not silently resolved)

- **θυμός = "heart"** (5.126 ᾧ θυμῷ, 5.191 θυμὸς … σιδήρεος). Row 278 of the table (θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ) says θυμός is "kept 'spirit' throughout". The owner-approved pilot, however, uses "heart" for θυμός (ὃν κατὰ θυμόν "in his own heart", 1.4), and so do fixed rows (κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν "in mind and in heart") and the shipped 5.157 that this part must repeat ("racking his heart"). I followed the pilot. The table contradicts itself here, and someone should settle it.
- **ἀέκητι σέθεν** (5.177): I rendered it "against your will", matching the shipped ἀέκητι σέθεν at 3.213. The sense is hard (it may be "in spite of you, whatever you urge"), and the note says so.
- **5.158 lower-cased**: the shipped line opens a sentence ("Toward the unharvested sea …"). Here it continues one, so `l` reads "toward the unharvested sea he kept gazing, tears pouring." and is otherwise verbatim. The `i` has to rebuild the whole sentence, and it keeps the shipped phrases ("kept gazing out over the sea that yields no harvest, pouring out his tears").
- **φράσσομαι** (5.188): the note calls it "most naturally a future". A short-vowel aorist subjunctive is also possible.
- **ἠνώγειν** (5.112): the note takes it as the -ειν variant of the third singular pluperfect.
- **Hermes vs Calypso on the wreck**: the notes at 5.108 and 5.130 point out that Hermes blames Athena's storm and Calypso blames Zeus's thunderbolt. Both claims come from this part's own text.
